item.title: What Happens When the Dopamine Hit Goes Away?
item.description:
I have been thinking about the dopamine hits we get from troubleshooting, debugging and getting programmes just right. We don’t get paid for this, so it features much less in the conversation about why people do this work.

Why a lot of us got here

A lot of people, especially millennials who came to tech from working on things on their own, got here because of the sense of achievement that tech gave us. We managed to get things working. That dopamine hit, that sense of accomplishment, of getting things done, of having control over all aspects of it.

It was our responsibility, our doing, that determined whether the thing worked or not. There were no external influences. It was solely our skill, knowledge and ability that decided whether we got the thing working. And we derived our happiness from that. We derived our happiness from a job well done.

There were extrinsic motivators for sure. It paid well. It’s a good job. We got to work with smart people. But ultimately, I think the thing that clinched the deal was that we got a nice little dopamine hit whenever we managed to get the thing done, whatever the thing was: writing a program, troubleshooting a system, fixing a bug.

The loop we lived in

To understand this, you have to understand the psychology of software development, at least as we practiced it before the advent of LLMs and agentic AI.

The loop went like this. You were faced with a problem, and then you went on a bit of a journey to explore and understand what exactly the problem was. You tried to nail it down, work out how to get the thing done, and do some research on prior art. You got your mind ready and got all the information in place. You used whatever note-taking system or knowledge base you had to organise your thoughts. You got your ducks in a row.

It was all the prep work. This is akin to any artisan getting the raw materials ready, getting their tools ready and making a plan, before starting the execution.

Then you started attacking the problem. You implemented a little bit of the solution and tested it out. You wrote a unit test, you wrote an integration test, you made it pass, and then you did it over and over again until you got to the place where you wanted to be, until you were satisfied with it.

Flow was the holy grail

You got into the flow. The flow state was the holy grail, it was what we were chasing. How long you could stay in the flow was the mark of how good you were as a programmer. That was the achievement we were all chasing, and that was the dopamine hit. When you got out of the flow, it didn’t matter how much time had passed. If you got there, that day felt productive.

Joel Spolsky talks about this in one of his blogs, Where do These People Get Their (Unoriginal) Ideas?

It was not an end goal by itself, but it mattered a lot to who we were. It was tied to our identity. We made knowing jokes about it. We talked about how to get better techniques and tools for achieving the flow state. It was almost a goal in itself. It didn’t matter to the business, but for the individual it mattered a lot. For your own satisfaction, it mattered a lot.

What LLMs and agentic AI change

With LLMs, that is going away. With agentic AI and whatnot, there’s your skill atrophy and all that. That’s fine to worry about, and it needs to be a concern we talk about. But the conversation about what losing this intrinsic motivator will do to people seems to get buried under the mountain of other things we’re talking about.

And that incentive structure going away is a fundamental change to how we operate. What sort of incentive structure is in place for us now? How do you explain to the newcomers, the new software engineers, how this works? And what do we replace it with?

What we have instead is short interactions with an agentic AI, followed by long spells of reviewing the system and the code. The problem with the review phase is that you’re not producing anything. You’re not generating, so there’s no sense of accomplishment. It’s a chore, a drudge that you have to go through. Even though it’s something big, something substantial, there’s no accomplishment at the end of it.

The questions I keep coming back to

I wonder how this is going to go for people.

  • How would people derive satisfaction from doing this work?
  • Would their job satisfaction be lower?
  • I’ve always felt we had a unique position, where we enjoyed the work we do a lot. Would this become menial, trudging work, like other sorts of admin work?
  • If that is the case, how would this field even attract new people?
  • What is going to be our incentive? Money can only motivate people so much, as research has shown.

I don’t know what’s going to happen, but it’s fascinating to think about.

item.title: MCP vs SDK: Two Paths to LLM-Powered Extensibility
item.description:
MCP vs SDK: Two Paths to LLM‑Powered Extensibility

Two different ways to let your app work better for people (and their AI helpers).

From “software eats the world” to AI in the loop

When software started taking over everything, the real winners were the people who could make it do exactly what they wanted. That usually meant writing code - either a whole new app, or scripts inside an existing one. Which meant you had to be a programmer - a costly, time consuming affair that needed significant investment from users point of view. In every office/workplace that is not a software shop, you would know the one person who is the designated computer whisperer, the genius who knows the right incantations to make the computer do exactly what they want. In reality they are comfortable with the operation system, tools and a couple of scripting languages.

And then came the rise of user‑programmable environments. Lotus 1‑2‑3, for example, had macros as far back as the late ’80s, and Excel carried that torch with VBA. These weren’t just nice extras - they opened up whole new ways for people to bend the software to their own needs. This meant now you did not need to program everything from the ground up. These tools were end user software as well so there was some functionality already built in - infact a heck of a lot of functionality. But more importantly they allowed those functionality to be used as building blocks now.

This paved the way for a generation of end‑user programmable tools. Some evolved into full scripting environments inside mainstream apps. elisp is probably the most famous of these leading to many programmers who wax lyrical about how powerful it makes emacs (now you know which editor I prefer!). And some others spun off into no‑code platforms. No‑code is an interesting branch - it promises power without syntax, but it’s still unclear where it fits in the long run. It sits somewhere between “use what’s shipped” and “write a proper program,” but it’s not always clear how far it can take you.

At the heart of all this is one goal: let people get more out of the software you build. The stock functionality matters, sure, but in the age of LLMs, it matters just as much - maybe more - what hooks you give those AI‑powered tools to work with. People are going to be using them, and the more effectively those tools can drive your software, the more value your users will be able to extract.

I’m not saying replace your app with a language - ship the app you want to ship. But alongside that, think hard about what you enable the AI layer to do. If people are using a tool, you should make sure they can use it in the most effective way possible - whether they’re typing commands themselves or letting an AI do it for them.

From that perspective, there are two main ways forward:

  1. Expose an MCP server (or something similar) so an LLM can directly call into your app using a set of defined commands.
  2. Expose a programmable interface (SDK, DSL, low‑code) and let the LLM write the code that uses it.

Think AWS CLI vs AWS SDK - one’s a quick, command‑driven way in; the other’s a fully programmable toolkit.

MCP: a command surface for AI

What it is: You publish a set of clear, well‑defined actions: create_invoice, fetch_customer, transcode_audio, etc. The LLM calls them, your app runs them, and returns results.

Pros

  • Quick wins: Easy for an LLM to use without setup.
  • Safety first: You control what’s exposed, check inputs, and keep risky stuff locked down.
  • Predictable: The API contract is stable even if internals change.
  • Great for operations: Easy to log, audit, and trace exactly what happened.

Cons

  • Less composable: You can chain calls, but big workflows get clunky without another layer.
  • Feature creep: Power users ask for more and more commands.
  • Logic ends up elsewhere: The “brains” live in the orchestrator, not your app.

Good for: Repetitive tasks, customer support tools, CRUD operations, data lookups.

SDK/DSL: let AIs write “real” programs

What it is: A language binding, DSL, or low‑code setup that the LLM can write to build workflows and automations.

Pros

  • Fully composable: Loops, conditionals, abstractions - you can build proper systems.
  • Durable: Code can be saved, versioned, and reused.
  • Plays well with others: Easy to integrate with the rest of a tech stack.

Cons

  • More friction: Needs an environment, keys, maybe a bit of human literacy.
  • Security risks: Arbitrary code execution means you need guardrails.
  • Higher support load: You’re now running a developer platform.

Good for: Data pipelines, complex automations, custom integrations.

Why most mature platforms end up with both

CLI‑style (MCP) is great for quick wins. SDK‑style is great for deep integrations. People (and AIs) often start with one‑off commands and then graduate to building proper systems. The key is keeping boundaries clear:

  • MCP tools: coarse‑grained, task‑focused, with well‑defined inputs and outputs.
  • SDK/DSL: small, composable primitives that can be wired together any way the user needs.

I predict that most mature software products/platforms will end up with both.

Checklist

For MCP

  • Ship tools for your top 10 “jobs to be done.”
  • Lock down inputs/outputs with schemas.
  • Include dry‑run mode, idempotency, and audit logs.
  • Scope permissions tightly.

For SDK/DSL

  • Keep functions small and focused.
  • Provide examples and a quick dev loop.
  • Version properly and ship migration guides.
  • Include typed clients and golden‑path recipes.

Example for ERP/Order Management System

MCP tool:

{
  "name": "generate_invoice",
  "description": "Create and email a PDF invoice for a paid order",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "order_id": { "type": "string" },
      "send_email": { "type": "boolean" }
    },
    "required": ["order_id"]
  }
}

SDK:

inv = client.invoice.create(order_id)
inv.add_memo("Rush delivery")
if total(inv) > 5000:
    inv.require_po()
inv.email(to=accounting_alias)

Same capability, different ergonomics: MCP is do the thing; SDK is build the process.

Final thought

Start small with MCP for quick wins. Build out an SDK for the power users. Link the two so people can move from “just run this” to “build me the workflow” without friction.
